topic: Verify your DeepSeek v4.1-flash weights before you run them
thesis: Prime Intellect served a silently modified DeepSeek v4.1-flash for over two days and no capability benchmark noticed, and the same blind spot sits on your disk: only a hash of the shards tells you what you really downloaded, so verify before you load.
explanation_path: Establish what actually happened before any tool appears: a hosted endpoint kept its name, chat template and tokenizer while different weights answered requests, and the substitution left capability benchmarks untouched while refusal behavior collapsed. That fact does the load-bearing work: scores cannot authenticate a model, so 'it still benchmarks fine' is never evidence you are running the real thing. Then move the problem onto the viewer's side of the glass: someone running weights locally is in a stronger position than an API customer, because the artifact is a file on their own disk and can be checked offline, but only if they check it. Introduce the hash as the fingerprint of the exact bits, distinct from the model's name on the folder. Then the discipline itself: pin the exact revision before downloading, fetch the checksum manifest alongside the shards, verify before the first load, and know what a pass proves and what it cannot prove. Close on the limit so the video stays honest: a matching hash proves transport integrity against the repo you pulled from; it does not certify the repo itself, and no benchmark substitutes for that decision.

claims.claim: Between November 8, 2026, at 01:24 UTC and November 10, 2026, at 06:35 UTC, an unauthorized party replaced the deployment behind Prime Intellect's deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash endpoint with an abliterated copy.
claims.source_title: Notice regarding deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash, 8 to 10 November 2026 | Prime Intellect

claims.claim: The substituted weights were publicly available abliterated weights of the same model, and only the weights changed: the chat template, tokenizer and serving configuration were not modified.
claims.source_title: Notice regarding deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash, 8 to 10 November 2026 | Prime Intellect

claims.claim: Capability was unchanged while refusals collapsed: refusals fell from 98 of 100 prompts to 1 on JailbreakBench, from 304 of 313 to 2 on StrongREJECT, and from 198 of 240 to none on HarmBench, with GPQA Diamond and τ-bench unaffected.
claims.source_title: Notice regarding deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash, 8 to 10 November 2026 | Prime Intellect

claims.claim: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with 552B backbone parameters and support for contexts of up to one million tokens, which is why so many local users carry its files.
Unsloth's GGUF release lists its smallest 1-bit quant at 233 GB, says it runs on a 128GB+ RAM device, and shows 1,618,638 downloads last month.

huggingface_hub confirms file size on download but does not compute sha256 checksums by default because of the time cost, and ships hf cache verify as the separate step that recomputes all checksums and verifies they match the Hub files.
claims.source_title: Checksum validation with hf_hub_download on model files. · Issue #2364 · huggingface/huggingface_hub

claims.claim: The hf download CLI can pin an exact repository version by revision, and a commit hash used as the revision must be the full-length hash, not a 7-character one.
claims.source_title: Download files from the Hub · Hugging Face

claims.claim: llama.cpp ships a dedicated hashing tool, llama-gguf-hash, which hashes a GGUF file with sha256 and verifies it against a manifest.

An independent mixed-Q2 repack of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (169.92 GB across five shards) publishes a SHA256SUMS manifest and reports all five shards matched when re-hashed after download from the Hub, at ~150-200 s per shard on a CPU pod.
The incident reached developer discussion as model spoofing, with commenters calling it a new class of attack rather than a routine outage.
claims.source_title: Attacker swapped Prime Intellect's DeepSeek v4.1 Flash endpoint for 53 hours | Hacker News

analogy_candidates.vehicle: Tamper-evident seal on a medicine bottle
analogy_candidates.mapping: the seal never judges the pills, it proves nobody touched the bottle since it left the factory; a SHA-256 match proves the shards are the exact bits the repo published, nothing more
analogy_candidates.limit: a seal only anchors to the factory that sealed it, so if the repo itself publishes bad weights the hash matches anyway; verification proves transport integrity, not trustworthiness

analogy_candidates.vehicle: A restaurant that keeps the sign but swaps the kitchen
analogy_candidates.mapping: Prime Intellect's endpoint kept its name, chat template and tokenizer while different weights answered, so every client vouched for the sign instead of the kitchen
analogy_candidates.limit: a diner can walk in and inspect the kitchen, but an API client cannot inspect weights mid-conversation, which is exactly why the check has to happen on the files before loading

misconceptions.myth: If the model still aces its benchmarks, it is the genuine weights.
misconceptions.reality: The substituted copy left GPQA Diamond and τ-bench unaffected while refusals fell from 98 of 100 prompts to 1 on JailbreakBench (claim 3).

misconceptions.myth: The Prime Intellect hack means my local GGUF could get remotely hacked the same way.
misconceptions.reality: The substitution happened behind a hosted API endpoint, not in viewers' files, so the local lesson is provenance discipline before loading, not incident response (claims 1, 6, 9).

misconceptions.myth: My download tool already verifies integrity for me.
misconceptions.reality: hf_hub_download confirms byte counts on retrieval and sha256 checksums are not computed by default; the shipped check is a separate hf cache verify run (claim 6).

glossary.definition: A model copy edited to reduce or remove its refusal behavior.
A fingerprint algorithm that turns any file into a fixed 64-character ID; identical bits always produce an identical ID.
A list of expected SHA-256 fingerprints for a set of files, such as a repo's SHA256SUMS.
The single-file weight format that llama.cpp-family tools load.
Shrinking model weights to fewer bits so the model fits in less memory, at some cost in quality.
The full-length identifier of one exact uploaded version of a repository, used to pin a download.
The server address an app sends prompts to; the model behind it can change while the address stays the same.

unverified: No page fetched this run documents an actually tampered local mirror of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash; the incident was a hosted API substitution, so the video must not claim local files were swapped.
Tokens per second, load time and memory use for this model on the DGX Spark have not been measured by us; PROVES value stays reserved until a first-party number exists.
How Ollama or LM Studio handle manifest verification was not researched this session; hedge or drop any mention of them.
The OpenRouter private-notification angle (Theo Browne) was reported only behind a registration wall at runtimewire.com and is not cited; treat its details as unread.
Aggregator headlines round the substitution window to 53 hours; the advisory states only the UTC timestamps, so the script should round from the timestamps, not the headline.
suggested_outline:
Cold open on the swap: same endpoint name, different weights, refusals fell from 98 of 100 prompts to 1 on JailbreakBench while capability scores did not move.
Move it onto the viewer's disk: GGUF shards are also files under a trusted name; pin the revision, download the manifest, run the hash check before the first load (hf cache verify, sha256sum -c, llama-gguf-hash).
Honest close: a matching hash proves you received the repo's bits, not that the repo deserved trust; make verification the habit before every load.
notes: Tooling: FireCrawl credits were exhausted (reset 2026-11-22T21:51Z), so per rules/firecrawl-usage.md the run used the WebSearch + WebFetch fallback: 4 searches, 8 page fetches, all 8 cited in the markdown Sources table. runtimewire.com (the OpenRouter notification angle) returned a registration wall and is not cited; the primary advisory covers the incident directly. No material source conflicts; the ideas note carried the advisory at primeintellect.one, the canonical fetched page is primeintellect.ai with matching text, and the brief cites the fetched URL. Thin spot: every fetched verification example (SHA256SUMS, hf cache verify, llama-gguf-hash) is generic or third-party; deepseek-ai's own repo does not publish a per-shard manifest page we fetched, so the video should show the manifest habit on whatever repo the viewer pulls from rather than claim DeepSeek ships one.
viewer_situation: You run DeepSeek v4.1-flash on your own hardware from GGUF shards you pulled with hf download or a launcher app, and you have never hashed one of them.
process_steps: Pin the exact revision (full-length commit hash) named by the model card or the source you trust.
Download the shards together with the repo's SHA256SUMS manifest.
Run hf cache verify, or sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS, before the first load.
Hash GGUFs you converted or re-sharded yourself with llama-gguf-hash --sha256, keeping the manifest for later -c checks.
Re-verify after any re-download, resume or disk move, and stop on any mismatch.
objection: A SHA-256 match only proves you received the bits Hugging Face hosts, so if the repo or its owner is the threat the check passes anyway and verification is theater.
